She went [[motifs/home|home]] very happy. The morning had answered all her hopes, and

the evening of the following day was now the object of expectation, the

future good. What gown and what head-dress she should wear on the

occasion became her chief concern. She cannot be justified in it. Dress

is at all times a frivolous distinction, and excessive solicitude about

it often destroys its own aim. Catherine knew all this very [[motifs/well|well]]; her

great aunt had read her a lecture on the subject only the Christmas

before; and yet she lay awake ten minutes on Wednesday [[motifs/night|night]] debating

between her spotted and her tamboured muslin, and nothing but the

shortness of the [[motifs/time|time]] prevented her buying a new one for the evening.

This would have been an error in judgment, great though not uncommon,

from which one of the other sex rather than her own, a brother rather

than a great aunt, might have warned her, for man only can be aware of

the insensibility of man towards a new gown. It would be mortifying to

the feelings of many ladies, could they be made to understand how

little the heart of man is affected by what is costly or new in their

attire; how little it is biased by the texture of their muslin, and how

unsusceptible of peculiar tenderness towards the spotted, the sprigged,

the mull, or the jackonet. Woman is fine for her own satisfaction

alone. No man will admire her the more, no woman will like her the

better for it. Neatness and fashion are enough for the former, and a

something of shabbiness or impropriety will be most endearing to the

latter. But not one of these [[motifs/grave|grave]] reflections troubled the

tranquillity of Catherine.



She entered the rooms on Thursday evening with feelings very different

from what had attended her thither the Monday before. She had then been

exulting in her engagement to Thorpe, and was now chiefly anxious to

avoid his sight, lest he should engage her again; for though she could

not, dared not expect that Mr. Tilney should ask her a third [[motifs/time|time]] to

[[motifs/dance|dance]], her wishes, hopes, and plans all centred in nothing less. Every

young lady may feel for my heroine in this critical moment, for every

young lady has at some [[motifs/time|time]] or other known the same agitation. All have

been, or at least all have believed themselves to be, in danger from

the pursuit of someone whom they wished to avoid; and all have been

anxious for the attentions of someone whom they wished to please. As

soon as they were joined by the Thorpes, Catherine’s agony began; she

fidgeted about if [[characters/john-thorpe|John Thorpe]] came towards her, hid herself as much as

possible from his view, and when he spoke to her pretended not to hear

him. The cotillions were over, the country-dancing beginning, and she

saw nothing of the Tilneys.



“Do not be frightened, my dear Catherine,” whispered [[characters/isabella|Isabella]], “but I

am really going to [[motifs/dance|dance]] with your brother again. I declare positively

it is quite shocking. I tell him he ought to be ashamed of himself, but

you and John must keep us in countenance. Make haste, my dear creature,

and come to us. John is just walked off, but he will be back in a

moment.”



Catherine had neither [[motifs/time|time]] nor inclination to answer. The others walked

away, [[characters/john-thorpe|John Thorpe]] was still in view, and she gave herself up for lost.

That she might not appear, however, to observe or expect him, she kept

her eyes intently fixed on her fan; and a [[concepts/self|self]]-condemnation for her

folly, in supposing that among such a crowd they should even meet with

the Tilneys in any reasonable [[motifs/time|time]], had just passed through her mind,

when she suddenly found herself addressed and again solicited to [[motifs/dance|dance]],

by Mr. Tilney himself. With what sparkling eyes and ready motion she

granted his request, and with how pleasing a flutter of heart she went

with him to the set, may be easily imagined. To escape, and, as she

believed, so narrowly escape [[characters/john-thorpe|John Thorpe]], and to be asked, so

immediately on his joining her, asked by Mr. Tilney, as if he had

sought her on purpose!—it did not appear to her that life could supply

any greater felicity.



Scarcely had they worked themselves into the quiet possession of a

place, however, when her attention was claimed by [[characters/john-thorpe|John Thorpe]], who

stood behind her. “Heyday, Miss Morland!” said he. “What is the meaning

of this? I thought you and I were to [[motifs/dance|dance]] together.”



“I [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] you should think so, for you never asked me.”



“That is a good one, by Jove! i asked you as soon as I came into the

of dancing with _you_, and I firmly believe you were engaged to me ever

since Monday. Yes; I remember, I asked you while you were waiting in

“By heavens, if they do not, I will kick them out of the room for

blockheads. What chap have you there?” Catherine satisfied his

curiosity. “Tilney,” he repeated. “Hum—I do not know him. A good figure

of a man; [[motifs/well|well]] put together. Does he want a [[motifs/horse|horse]]? Here is a friend of

mine, Sam Fletcher, has got one to sell that would suit anybody. A

famous clever animal for the [[motifs/road|road]]—only forty guineas. I had fifty minds

to buy it myself, for it is one of my maxims always to buy a good [[motifs/horse|horse]]

when I meet with one; but it would not answer my purpose, it would not

do for the field. I would give any money for a real good hunter. I have

three now, the best that ever were backed. I would not take eight

hundred guineas for them. Fletcher and I mean to get a house in

Leicestershire, against the next season. It is so d—— uncomfortable,

living at an inn.”



This was the last sentence by which he could weary Catherine’s

attention, for he was just then borne off by the resistless pressure of

a long string of passing ladies. Her partner now drew near, and said,

“That gentleman would have put me out of patience, had he stayed with

you half a minute longer. He has no business to withdraw the attention

of my partner from me. We have entered into a contract of mutual

agreeableness for the space of an evening, and all our agreeableness

belongs solely to each other for that [[motifs/time|time]]. Nobody can fasten

themselves on the notice of one, without injuring the rights of the

other. I consider a country-[[motifs/dance|dance]] as an emblem of [[motifs/marriage|marriage]]. Fidelity

and complaisance are the principal duties of both; and those men who do

not choose to [[motifs/dance|dance]] or marry themselves, have no business with the

partners or wives of their neighbours.”



“But they are such very different things!”



“—That you think they cannot be compared together.”



“To be sure not. People that marry can never part, but must go and keep

house together. People that [[motifs/dance|dance]] only stand opposite each other in a

long room for half an hour.”



“And such is your definition of matrimony and dancing. Taken in that

light certainly, their resemblance is not striking; but I think I could

place them in such a view. You will allow, that in both, man has the

advantage of choice, woman only the power of refusal; that in both, it

is an engagement between man and woman, formed for the advantage of

each; and that when once entered into, they belong exclusively to each

other till the moment of its dissolution; that it is their duty, each

to endeavour to give the other no cause for wishing that he or she had

bestowed themselves elsewhere, and their best interest to keep their

own imaginations from wandering towards the perfections of their

neighbours, or fancying that they should have been better off with

anyone else. You will allow all this?”



“Yes, to be sure, as you state it, all this sounds very [[motifs/well|well]]; but still

they are so very different. I cannot look upon them at all in the same

light, nor think the same duties belong to them.”



“In one respect, there certainly is a difference. In [[motifs/marriage|marriage]], the man

is supposed to provide for the support of the woman, the woman to make

the [[motifs/home|home]] agreeable to the man; he is to purvey, and she is to smile.

But in dancing, their duties are exactly changed; the agreeableness,

the compliance are expected from him, while she furnishes the fan and

the lavender [[motifs/water|water]]. _That_, I suppose, was the difference of duties

which struck you, as rendering the conditions incapable of comparison.”



“No, indeed, I never thought of that.”



“Then I am quite at a loss. One thing, however, I must observe. This

disposition on your side is rather alarming. You totally disallow any

similarity in the obligations; and may I not thence infer that your

notions of the duties of the dancing state are not so strict as your

partner might wish? Have I not reason to [[concepts/fear|fear]] that if the gentleman who

spoke to you just now were to return, or if any other gentleman were to

address you, there would be nothing to restrain you from conversing

with him as long as you chose?”



“Mr. Thorpe is such a very particular friend of my brother’s, that if

he talks to me, I must talk to him again; but there are hardly three

young men in the room besides him that I have any acquaintance with.”



“And is that to be my only security? Alas, alas!”



“Nay, I am sure you cannot have a better; for if I do not know anybody,

it is impossible for me to talk to them; and, besides, I do not _want_

to talk to anybody.”



“Now you have given me a security worth having; and I shall proceed

with [[concepts/courage|courage]]. Do you find Bath as agreeable as when I had the [[concepts/honour|honour]] of

making the inquiry before?”



“Yes, quite—more so, indeed.”



“More so! take care, or you will forget to be tired of it at the proper

[[motifs/time|time]]. You ought to be tired at the end of six weeks.”



“I do not think I should be tired, if I were to stay here six months.”



“Bath, compared with [[settings/london|London]], has little variety, and so everybody finds

out every year. ‘For six weeks, I allow Bath is pleasant enough; but

beyond _that_, it is the most tiresome place in the world.’ You would

be told so by people of all descriptions, who come regularly every

last because they can afford to stay no longer.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], other people must judge for themselves, and those who go to

village in the country, can never find greater sameness in such a place

as this than in my own [[motifs/home|home]]; for here are a variety of amusements, a

“Mio caro Sam Fletcher, ne ho uno da vendere che andrebbe bene a chiunque.”

Un famoso e intelligente animale per le strade, solo quaranta ghinee. Ne avrei volute cinquanta.

Per comprarlo io stesso, perché uno dei miei principi fondamentali è sempre quello di acquistare un buon [[motifs/horse|cavallo]].

Quando incontro qualcuno… ma non serve ai miei scopi.

“Un vero cacciatore… darei qualsiasi somma per averne uno.”

Tre ora… i migliori che siano mai stati sostenuti. Non prenderei nemmeno otto.

Cento ghinee per loro. Fletcher ed io intendiamo comprare una >casa.

Leicestershire, contro la prossima stagione… È davvero scomodo.

"Vivere in una locanda."



Questa fu l’ultima frase con cui riuscì ad stancare Catherine

Attenzione: in quel momento fu portato via dalla pressione irresistibile…

“Una lunga serie di signore che passavano… Il suo compagno si avvicinò e disse…”

“Quel signore avrebbe finito per farmi perdere la pazienza, se fosse rimasto…”

Ancora mezzo minuto… Non ha alcun diritto di distogliere l’attenzione.

Il segreto del mio partner

Per una serata intera… tutta la nostra gentilezza e affabilità.

Appartengono esclusivamente l’uno all’altro in quel [[motifs/time|momento]]. Nessuno può separarli.

"#Notificare qualcuno senza violare i suoi diritti"

Altro. Considero la danza nazionale un simbolo del [[motifs/marriage|mattrimono]]. Fedeltà.

Obbedienza e compiacimento sono i principali doveri di entrambi; e coloro che li adempiono…

Non scegliere di [[motifs/dance|ballare]] o di sposarsi significa non avere nulla a che fare con.

“Compagni o mogli dei loro vicini”.



“Ma sono cose davvero molto diverse!”



“—Perché pensi che non possano essere paragonati tra loro.”



“Assolutamente no. Le persone che si sposano non possono mai separarsi, ma devono restare insieme per sempre.”

Vivere insieme in una casa. Le persone che [[motifs/dance|danzano]] si mettono semplicemente una di fronte all’altra.

“Una lunga stanza… per mezz’ora.”



“E questa è dunque la vostra definizione di matrimonio e danza… Se così si interpreta…”

“Certo, la somiglianza non è evidente… ma credo di poter…”

"Posizionarli in modo che… Voi ammetterete che, in entrambi i casi, l’uomo abbia…"

Il vantaggio della scelta: solo alle donne il potere di rifiutare; in entrambi i casi…

Il titolo si riferisce all’atto di impegnarsi reciprocamente tra un uomo e una donna, al fine di ottenere benefici reciproci.

Ognuno di essi; e una volta entrati in quel contesto, appartengono esclusivamente a ciascuno di loro.

“Altri fino al momento della loro dissoluzione; è loro dovere, ciascuno…”

Cercare di non dare all’altro motivo di desiderare che…

Si erano recati altrove, e il loro meglio interesse consisteva nel rimanere lì…

Trattenere le proprie immaginazioni lontane dai sentieri che portano alla perfezione

Vicini… o l’illusione che avrebbero potuto avere una vita migliore

“Qualcun altro… Voi permetterete davvero tutto questo?”



“Sì, certamente, come tu dici, tutto questo sembra molto [[motifs/well|buono]]; ma comunque, ”

“Sono così diversi… Non riesco affatto a considerarli allo stesso modo.”

“Non pensare mai che siano loro ad avere tali doveri.”



“Da un certo punto di vista, c’è sicuramente una differenza. Nel [[motifs/marriage|matrimonio]], l’uomo, ”

Titolo:  
Dovrebbe fornire il sostegno alla donna, affinché lei possa…

La [[motifs/home|casa]] è adatta a quell’uomo; lui si occuperà di provvedere alle necessità quotidiane, e lei dovrà sorridere.

Ma nella danza, i loro ruoli cambiano completamente; l’armonia…

“Si prevede che lui adotti comportamenti conformi alle aspettative, mentre lei fornisce il ventaglio…”

L’acqua alla lavanda. Quello, suppongo, fosse la differenza nei compiti loro assegnati.

“Quello che vi ha colpito è stato il fatto che tali condizioni rendessero impossibile qualsiasi tipo di confronto.”



"No, davvero, non ci avevo mai pensato."



“Allora sono davvero senza sapere cosa fare… Tuttavia, una cosa devo osservare.”

Una disposizione piuttosto allarmante da parte tua… Rifiuti completamente qualsiasi possibilità…

Titolo:  
“Similitudine nelle obbligazioni… E posso forse dedurre da ciò che…”

"Idee riguardo ai doveri dello ‘stato danzante’ non sono così rigorose come le tue..."

Il partner potrebbe volerlo. Non ho forse motivo di [[concepts/fear|temere]] che, se quel gentiluomo che.

Il messaggio che vi ho appena inviato era per chiedervi se voleste tornare, o se ci fosse qualche altro gentiluomo disposto a farlo…

Parlando con te, non ci sarebbe nulla che ti impedisse di conversare

“Rimarresti con lui per tutto il tempo che sceglierai tu?”



“Mr. Thorpe è un amico così particolare di mio fratello, che…”

“Lui parla con me, devo parlare di nuovo con lui… ma ci sono appena tre…”

Gli uomini giovani nella stanza, oltre a lui, che conosco.



“E questo dovrà essere il mio unico sostegno? Ahimè, ahimè…”



“No, sono sicuro che non si possa trovare nulla di meglio; perché se non conosco nessuno…”

“È impossibile per me parlare con loro; e, inoltre, non ne ho alcun desiderio.”

“Parlare con chiunque…”



Ora che mi avete fornito una garanzia davvero preziosa, procederò…

Con [[concepts/courage|coraggio]]. Trovi che Bath sia altrettanto piacevole come quando ho avuto l’onore di.

“Non è meglio fare prima delle indagini?”



“Sì, proprio… anzi, molto di più.”



“Ancora di più! Stai attento, altrimenti dimenticherai di stancartene nel momento giusto…”

[[motifs/time|tempo]]. Dopo sei settimane, dovresti essere stanco.



“Non credo che dovrei stancarmi, se rimanessi qui per sei mesi.”



“A Bath, rispetto a [[settings/london|Londra]], offre poche varietà, quindi tutti la trovano, ”

Ogni anno… Per sei settimane, trovo che Bath sia abbastanza piacevole; ma…

“Oltre a questo, è il posto più noioso del mondo.” Diresti…

Tutti dicono lo stesso, persone di ogni tipo, che vengono regolarmente…

Durante l’[[motifs/winter|inverno]], i loro sei settimani si allungano fino a dieci o dodici giorni, e poi se ne vanno.

“Ultimi perché non possono permettersi di restare oltre.”



“Beh, altre persone devono giudicare da sole, e coloro che vanno, ”

[[settings/london|Londra]] potrebbe non dare importanza a Bath. Ma io, che vivo in una piccola città tranquilla.

Villaggio di campagna: un luogo dove regna una perfetta uniformità

Più che nella mia stessa [[motifs/home|>casa]], perché qui ci sono molte forme di divertimento.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_11--part_04" data-title="Northanger Abbey — Chapter 10 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 11" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/clock,motif/dance,motif/home,motif/time,concept/fear,concept/longing,concept/poverty,concept/truth,character/bottom,character/general_tilney,character/isabella"></span>


variety of things to be seen and done all day long, which I can know

nothing of there.”



“You are not fond of the country.”



“Yes, I am. I have always lived there, and always been very happy. But

certainly there is much more sameness in a country life than in a Bath

life. One day in the country is exactly like another.”



“But then you spend your [[motifs/time|time]] so much more rationally in the country.”



“Do I?”



“Do you not?”



“I do not believe there is much difference.”



“Here you are in pursuit only of amusement all day long.”



“And so I am at [[motifs/home|home]]—only I do not find so much of it. I walk about

here, and so I do there; but here I see a variety of people in every

street, and there I can only go and call on Mrs. Allen.”



Mr. Tilney was very much amused.



“Only go and call on Mrs. Allen!” he repeated. “What a picture of

intellectual [[concepts/poverty|poverty]]! however, when you sink into this abyss again, you

will have more to say. You will be able to talk of Bath, and of all

that you did here.”



“Oh! yes. I shall never be in want of something to talk of again to

Mrs. Allen, or anybody else. I really believe I shall always be talking

of Bath, when I am at [[motifs/home|home]] again—I _do_ like it so very much. If I

could but have Papa and Mamma, and the rest of them here, I suppose I

should be too happy! james’s coming (my eldest brother) is quite

delightful—and especially as it turns out that the very family we are

just got so intimate with are his intimate friends already. Oh! who can

ever be tired of Bath?”



“Not those who bring such fresh feelings of every sort to it as you do.

But papas and mammas, and brothers, and intimate friends are a good

deal gone by, to most of the frequenters of Bath—and the honest relish

of balls and plays, and everyday sights, is past with them.”



Here their conversation closed, the demands of the [[motifs/dance|dance]] becoming now

too importunate for a divided attention.



Soon after their reaching the [[characters/bottom|bottom]] of the set, Catherine perceived

herself to be earnestly regarded by a gentleman who stood among the

lookers-on, immediately behind her partner. He was a very handsome man,

of a commanding aspect, past the bloom, but not past the vigour of

life; and with his eye still directed towards her, she saw him

presently address Mr. Tilney in a familiar whisper. Confused by his

notice, and blushing from the [[concepts/fear|fear]] of its being excited by something

wrong in her appearance, she turned away her head. But while she did

so, the gentleman retreated, and her partner, coming nearer, said, “I

see that you guess what I have just been asked. That gentleman knows

your name, and you have a right to know his. It is [[characters/general-tilney|General Tilney]], my

father.”



Catherine’s answer was only “Oh!”—but it was an “Oh!” expressing

everything needful: attention to his words, and perfect reliance on

their [[concepts/truth|truth]]. With real interest and strong admiration did her eye now

follow the General, as he moved through the crowd, and “How handsome a

family they are!” was her secret remark.



In chatting with Miss Tilney before the evening concluded, a new source

of felicity arose to her. She had never taken a country walk since her

arrival in Bath. Miss Tilney, to whom all the commonly frequented

environs were familiar, spoke of them in terms which made her all

eagerness to know them too; and on her openly fearing that she might

find nobody to go with her, it was proposed by the brother and sister

that they should join in a walk, some morning or other. “I shall like

it,” she cried, “beyond anything in the world; and do not let us put it

off—let us go to-morrow.” This was readily agreed to, with only a

proviso of Miss Tilney’s, that it did not rain, which Catherine was

sure it would not. At twelve o’[[motifs/clock|clock]], they were to call for her in

Pulteney Street; and “Remember—twelve o’[[motifs/clock|clock]],” was her parting speech

to her new friend. Of her other, her older, her more established

friend, [[characters/isabella|Isabella]], of whose fidelity and worth she had enjoyed a

fortnight’s experience, she scarcely saw anything during the evening.

Yet, though [[concepts/longing|longing]] to make her acquainted with her happiness, she

cheerfully submitted to the wish of Mr. Allen, which took them rather

early away, and her spirits danced within her, as she danced in her

chair all the way [[motifs/home|home]].


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Una varietà di cose da vedere e fare tutto il giorno, che posso conoscere…”

“Niente di tutto ciò.”



“Non ti piace molto la campagna…”



"Sì, lo sono. Ho sempre vissuto lì e sono sempre stata molto felice. Ma..."

Certo, nella vita di campagna c’è molto più uniformità rispetto a Bath.

“La vita… Un giorno in campagna è esattamente uguale ad un altro.”



“Ma allora trascorri il tuo [[motifs/time|tempo]] in modo molto più razionale in campagna.”



“Do I?”



“Non è vero?”



“Non credo ci sia molta differenza.”



“Qui si tratta soltanto di cercare divertimento per tutto il giorno.”



“E così sono a [[motifs/home|casa]], solo che non la trovo più come una volta. Vago avanti e indietro, ”

Qui, e così faccio anche lì; ma qui vedo una varietà di persone in ogni…

“Via della Strada… Lì non posso fare altro che andare a trovare la signora Allen.”



Il signor Tilney si divertì molto.



“Vai pure a far visita alla signora Allen!” ripeté. “Che quadro davvero…”

Povertà intellettuale. Tuttavia, quando ti ritrovi di nuovo in questo abisso, tu.

Avrà ancora molto da dire… Potrete parlare di Bath, e di tutto il resto.

“Per quello che hai fatto qui…”



“Ah sì… Ora non mi mancherà mai più argomento di cui parlare.”

La signora Allen… o chiunque altro. Sono davvero convinta che continuerò sempre a parlare di loro.

Di Bath, quando tornerò a [[motifs/home|casa]], mi piacerà davvero molto. Se io.

“Se solo avessi papà e mamma, e tutti gli altri qui con me…”

Sarà troppo felice… Arriva James, mio fratello maggiore.

Delizioso… soprattutto considerando che proprio quella famiglia, di cui stiamo parlando, si rivela essere…

Già così intimi con i suoi amici più cari… Oh, chi può…

“Si è mai stancati di Bath?”



“Non quelli che portano in esso tali sentimenti freschi e vari, come fai tu.”

“Ma papà e mamma, fratelli e amici intimi sono davvero importanti…”

“Un affare concluso, per la maggior parte dei frequentatori di Bath… e per coloro che apprezzano la sincerità”.

“Tutti i giochi, le feste e le scene quotidiane sono ormai passati…”



Ecco come terminò la loro conversazione; le richieste della [[motifs/dance|danza]] divennero ora.

Troppo insistente per essere preso in considerazione in un momento di distrazione.



Poco dopo essere arrivati in fondo al percorso, Catherine se ne rese conto.

Essere seriamente considerata da un gentiluomo che si trovava tra loro…

Ispettatori, immediatamente dietro la sua compagna… Era un uomo molto attraente.

Di un aspetto imponente, al di là del fiorente periodo, ma ancora pieno di vitalità

Titolo:  
La vita… e con lo sguardo ancora fisso su di lei, lo vide.

In quel momento, si rivolge al signor Tilney sussurrando in tono confidenziale… Confuso dal suo comportamento…

Notò, e arrossì per la [[concepts/fear|>paura]] che potesse essere eccitato da qualcosa.

“Con un aspetto che non le piaceva, girò la testa da un’altra parte… Ma mentre lo faceva…”

Il gentiluomo si allontanò, e la sua compagna, avvicinandosi, disse: “Io…”

Titolo:  
Vedi un po’ se riesci a indovinare cosa mi è stato appena chiesto… Quel signore lo sa.

Il tuo nome, e hai il diritto di conoscerne anche il suo. È [[characters/general-tilney|Generale Tilney]], il mio.

“Padre…”



La risposta di Catherine fu soltanto “Oh!”, ma un “Oh!” che esprimeva…

Tutto ciò che è necessario: attenzione alle sue parole e una perfetta fiducia in lui.

La loro [[concepts/truth|verità]]. Ora, con vero interesse e profonda ammirazione, i suoi occhi la osservavano.

“Segui il Generale mentre si muove tra la folla… Che bell’uomo!”

“Una famiglia, dopotutto, ”, era il suo commento segreto.



Durante la conversazione con la signorina Tilney, prima che la serata terminasse, emerse una nuova fonte…

Un senso di felicità la invase. Da allora, non aveva mai più fatto una passeggiata in campagna…

Arrivo a Bath. La signorina Tilney, che frequenta spesso i luoghi comunemente frequentati…

“Il luogo circostante le era familiare; ne parlava usando termini che la facevano sentire a casa…”

Desiderio ardente di conoscerli anch’essa; e lei, apertamente, temeva che potesse…

Non trovando nessuno con cui andare, fu il fratello e la sorella a proporle di partire insieme.

“Che si unissero a una passeggiata, una mattina o l’altra… Mi piacerebbe molto.”

“Non lo lasciate mai andare“, gridò, “è più importante di qualsiasi altra cosa al mondo… Non permetteteci di perderlo“.

“Domani andiamo,” fu proposto senza alcuna obiezione.

"La condizione posta da Miss Tilney: che non piovesse… e Catherine era…"

Certo che no. Alle dodici in punto, dovevano andarla a prendere.

Via Pulteney; e “Ricorda, le dodici in punto”, furono le sue ultime parole prima di andarsene.

“Al suo nuovo amico… Del suo altro, più anziano, più affermato…”

Amica mia, [[characters/isabella|Isabella]], di cui aveva apprezzato la fedeltà e il valore.

Dopo quell’esperienza durata due settimane, quasi non vedeva nulla durante la sera.

Tuttavia, nonostante il desiderio di farle conoscere la sua felicità, lei.

Con piacere si è adempiuto al desiderio del signor Allen… il che li ha resi abbastanza soddisfatti.

Partì presto, e il suo spirito danzava dentro di lei mentre ballava…

Seduto per tutto il tragitto fino a [[motifs/home|casa]].



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_12--part_01" data-title="Northanger Abbey — Chapter 11 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 12" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/clock,motif/night,motif/time,motif/window,concept/despair,concept/doubt,concept/hope,concept/wonder,setting/castle,character/isabella,character/john_thorpe"></span>


CHAPTER 11





The morrow brought a very sober-looking morning, the sun making only a

few efforts to appear, and Catherine augured from it everything most

favourable to her wishes. A bright morning so early in the year, she

allowed, would generally turn to rain, but a cloudy one foretold

improvement as the day advanced. She applied to Mr. Allen for

confirmation of her hopes, but Mr. Allen, not having his own skies and

barometer about him, declined giving any absolute promise of sunshine.

She applied to Mrs. Allen, and Mrs. Allen’s opinion was more positive.

“She had no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] in the world of its being a very fine day, if the

clouds would only go off, and the sun keep out.”



At about eleven o’[[motifs/clock|clock]], however, a few specks of small rain upon the

windows caught Catherine’s watchful eye, and “Oh! dear, I do believe it

will be wet,” broke from her in a most desponding tone.



“I thought how it would be,” said Mrs. Allen.



“No walk for me to-day,” sighed Catherine; “but perhaps it may come to

nothing, or it may hold up before twelve.”



“Perhaps it may, but then, my dear, it will be so dirty.”



“Oh! that will not signify; I never mind dirt.”



“No,” replied her friend very placidly, “I know you never mind dirt.”



After a short pause, “It comes on faster and faster!” said Catherine,

as she stood watching at a [[motifs/window|window]].



“So it does indeed. If it keeps raining, the streets will be very wet.”



“There are four umbrellas up already. How I hate the sight of an

umbrella!”



“They are disagreeable things to carry. I would much rather take a

chair at any [[motifs/time|time]].”



“It was such a nice-looking morning! i felt so convinced it would be

dry!”



“Anybody would have thought so indeed. There will be very few people in

the pump-room, if it rains all the morning. I [[concepts/hope|hope]] Mr. Allen will put

on his greatcoat when he goes, but I dare say he will not, for he had

rather do anything in the world than walk out in a greatcoat; I [[concepts/wonder|wonder]]

he should dislike it, it must be so comfortable.”



The rain continued—fast, though not heavy. Catherine went every five

minutes to the [[motifs/clock|clock]], threatening on each return that, if it still kept

on raining another five minutes, she would give up the matter as

hopeless. The [[motifs/clock|clock]] struck twelve, and it still rained. “You will not

be able to go, my dear.”



“I do not quite [[concepts/despair|despair]] yet. I shall not give it up till a quarter

after twelve. This is just the [[motifs/time|time]] of day for it to clear up, and I do

think it looks a little lighter. There, it is twenty minutes after

twelve, and now I _shall_ give it up entirely. Oh! that we had such

weather here as they had at Udolpho, or at least in Tuscany and the

south of France!—the [[motifs/night|night]] that poor St. Aubin died!—such beautiful

weather!”



At half past twelve, when Catherine’s anxious attention to the weather

was over and she could no longer claim any merit from its amendment,

the sky began voluntarily to clear. A gleam of sunshine took her quite

by surprise; she looked round; the clouds were parting, and she

instantly returned to the [[motifs/window|window]] to watch over and encourage the happy

appearance. Ten minutes more made it certain that a bright afternoon

would succeed, and justified the opinion of Mrs. Allen, who had “always

thought it would clear up.” But whether Catherine might still expect

her friends, whether there had not been too much rain for Miss Tilney

to venture, must yet be a question.



It was too dirty for Mrs. Allen to accompany her husband to the

pump-room; he accordingly set off by himself, and Catherine had barely

watched him down the street when her notice was claimed by the approach

of the same two open carriages, containing the same three people that

had surprised her so much a few mornings back.



“[[characters/isabella|Isabella]], my brother, and Mr. Thorpe, I declare! they are coming for

me perhaps—but I shall not go—I cannot go indeed, for you know Miss

Tilney may still call.” Mrs. Allen agreed to it. [[characters/john-thorpe|John Thorpe]] was soon

with them, and his voice was with them yet sooner, for on the stairs he

was calling out to Miss Morland to be quick. “Make haste! make haste!”

as he threw open the door. “Put on your hat this moment—there is no

[[motifs/time|time]] to be lost—we are going to Bristol. How d’ye do, Mrs. Allen?”



“To Bristol! is not that a great way off? But, however, I cannot go

with you to-day, because I am engaged; I expect some friends every

moment.” This was of course vehemently talked down as no reason at all;

Mrs. Allen was called on to second him, and the two others walked in,

to give their assistance. “My sweetest Catherine, is not this

delightful? We shall have a most heavenly drive. You are to thank your

brother and me for the scheme; it darted into our heads at

breakfast-[[motifs/time|time]], I verily believe at the same instant; and we should

have been off two hours ago if it had not been for this detestable

rain. But it does not signify, the nights are moonlight, and we shall

do delightfully. Oh! i am in such ecstasies at the thoughts of a little

country air and quiet! so much better than going to the Lower Rooms. We

shall drive directly to Clifton and dine there; and, as soon as dinner

is over, if there is [[motifs/time|time]] for it, go on to Kingsweston.”



“I [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] our being able to do so much,” said Morland.



“You croaking fellow!” cried Thorpe. “We shall be able to do ten times

more. Kingsweston! aye, and Blaize [[settings/castle|Castle]] too, and anything else we can

hear of; but here is your sister says she will not go.”



“Blaize [[settings/castle|Castle]]!” cried Catherine. “What is that?”



“The finest place in England—worth going fifty miles at any [[motifs/time|time]] to

see.”



“What, is it really a [[settings/castle|castle]], an old [[settings/castle|castle]]?”



“The oldest in the kingdom.”



“But is it like what one reads of?”



“Exactly—the very same.”



“But now really—are there towers and long galleries?”


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO 11





Il giorno seguente iniziò con una mattina molto serena; il sole splendeva debolmente…

Poche erano le tentativi di mostrarsi interessati, e Catherine ne dedusse tutto ciò che poteva significare…

Un mattino sereno e luminoso, così presto nell’anno… Lei…

Se permesso, di solito si trasformerebbe in pioggia… ma una nuvola scura presagiva il suo arrivo.

Con il passare delle ore, le cose miglioravano sempre di più. Lei chiese a Mr. Allen…

La conferma dei suoi speranze… ma il signor Allen, che non possedeva i propri “cieli”…

Il barometro intorno a lui indicava un peggioramento delle condizioni meteorologiche; non c'erano promesse certe di bel tempo.

Lei fece domanda a Madame Allen, e l’opinione di Madame Allen fu più positiva.

“Non aveva alcun [[concepts/doubt|>dubbio]] al mondo che fosse una giornata davvero meravigliosa, ”

“Le nuvole si sarebbero solo disperse, lasciando spazio al sole.”



Intorno alle undici in punto, tuttavia, alcune gocce di pioggia leggera cominciarono a cadere.

“Le finestre attirarono l’attenzione attenta di Catherine, e ‘Oh! mio Dio, ne sono sicura…’”

“Sarà bagnato, ”, disse lei con un tono estremamente scoraggiato.



“Pensavo a come sarebbe stato,” disse la signora Allen.



“Oggi non posso andare a fare una passeggiata“, sospirò Catherine; “ma forse, un giorno… potrà succedere“.

“Niente… altrimenti potrebbe non essere pronto prima delle dodici.”



“Forse sì, ma allora… caro mio, diventerà davvero molto sporco.”



“Ah! Non significa nulla… Non mi importa affatto la sporcizia.”



“Mai”, rispose la sua amica con grande calma, “so che a te non importa affatto la sporcizia”.



Dopo una breve pausa, “Si fa sempre più veloce!”, disse Catherine.

Mentre stava in piedi a guardare fuori dalla [[motifs/window|finestra]].



“Infatti. Se continua a piovere, le strade diventeranno molto bagnate.”



“Ci sono già quattro ombrelli aperti… Come odio quella vista.”

“Ombrello!”



“Sono cose sgradevoli da portare con sé… Preferirei di gran lunga…”

“Posso assumere la carica di presidente in qualsiasi momento.”



“Che bella mattina… Ero sicura che sarebbe stata davvero una giornata meravigliosa.”

“Secco!”



“Chiunque avrebbe potuto pensarlo davvero… Saranno poche le persone che…”

La sala delle pompe, se piove tutto il mattino. Spero che il signor Allen la utilizzi.

Sulla sua giacca quando se ne va, ma oserei dire che non lo farà, perché…

Preferirei fare qualsiasi cosa al mondo piuttosto che uscire indossando un grande cappotto. Mi chiedo davvero perché.

“Deve proprio non piacergli… Dev’essere davvero troppo comodo.”



La pioggia continuava… intensa, ma non troppo forte. Catherine usciva ogni cinque minuti…

Minuti mancavano all’[[motifs/clock|orologio]]; ad ogni ritorno minacciava che, se continuava a funzionare così.

Se avesse piovuto ancora per cinque minuti, avrebbe rinunciato all’idea.

Senza speranza. L’[[motifs/clock|orologio]] suonò le dodici, ma la pioggia continuava. “Non ce la farai, ”

“Potrai andare, mia cara.”



“Non sono ancora del tutto [[concepts/despair|disperato]]. Non mi arrenderò fino a che non sia trascorso un quarto, ”

Dopo le dodici. È proprio in questo momento della giornata che il tempo si schiarisce, e io lo so bene.

Titolo:  
“Pare un po’ più chiaro, vero? Ecco… sono passati venti minuti.”

Dodici… e ora lo abbandonerò del tutto. Oh! Se solo potessimo…

Il tempo qui è simile a quello di Udolpho… o almeno in Toscana e nelle zone circostanti.

A sud della Francia, quella [[motifs/night|notte]] in cui povero San Aubin morì, così bello.

“Tempo incerto…”



Alle dodici e mezza, mentre l’ansiosa attenzione di Catherine era rivolta al tempo…

La fase era terminata e lei non poteva più attribuirsi alcun merito per le modifiche apportate.

Il cielo iniziò spontaneamente a schiarirsi; un raggio di sole la illuminò completamente.

All’improvviso; si guardò intorno; le nuvole si stavano aprendo… e lei…

Tornò immediatamente alla [[motifs/window|finestra]] per vegliare su di loro e incoraggiarli in quel momento felice.

Aspetto… Dieci minuti in più furono sufficienti per confermare che si trattava di un pomeriggio luminoso e sereno.

Sarebbe riuscito, e avrebbe confermato l’opinione della signora Allen, che “sempre…”

“Pensavo che si schiarisse tutto…” Ma chissà se Catherine possa ancora aspettarselo…

I suoi amici… anche se forse pioveva troppo per la signorina Tilney

Per osare, bisogna ancora prendere in considerazione questa possibilità.



Era troppo sporco perché la signora Allen potesse accompagnare suo marito…

Bagno degli uomini; così si avviò da solo, e Catherine appena…

Lo ha seguito per tutta la strada, mentre qualcuno veniva a ritirare il suo avviso…

Titolo:  
Dei due stessi vagoni aperti, con le stesse tre persone a bordo…

Qualche mattina fa l’aveva sorpresa così tanto.



“[[characters/isabella|Isabella]], mio fratello e il signor Thorpe, li dichiaro: stanno arrivando!”

“Forse io… ma non andrò; davvero non posso andare, perché voi sapete, signorina…”

“Tilney potrebbe ancora chiamare,” concordò la signora Allen. Presto, [[characters/john-thorpe|John Thorpe]].

Con loro… e la sua voce era già con loro, ancora prima: perché sulle scale…

“Presto, signorina Morland… affrettatevi!”

“Mentre spalancava la porta, disse: ‘Metti subito il cappello… non c’è tempo da perdere.’”

Non c’è tempo da perdere; andiamo a Bristol. Come sta, signora Allen?



“Verso Bristol… non è una distanza troppo lunga? Comunque, non posso andare.”

Oggi non posso essere con te, perché sono impegnato; aspetto alcuni amici tra poco…

“Un momento…”, ma naturalmente questa richiesta fu immediatamente respinta come del tutto infondata.

La signora Allen fu invitata ad appoggiarlo, e gli altri due entrarono insieme.

“Per offrire il loro aiuto… Mia adorata Catherine, non è forse questo…”

Delizioso… Avremo un viaggio davvero meraviglioso. Dovete ringraziare voi stessi…

“Me e mio fratello: l’idea ci è venuta all’improvviso…”

Alle ore del breakfast, credo davvero che sia esattamente lo stesso istante. E dovremmo.

Se non fosse stato per questa cosa odiosa… sarei già tornato da due ore.

Pioggia… Ma questo non significa che le notti siano illuminate dalla luna, e che quindi…

Deliziosamente… Ah! Sono in estasi al solo pensiero di qualcosa di così piccolo e meraviglioso…

Aria di campagna e tranquillità… molto meglio che andare nelle “Lower Rooms”. Noi…

Si dirigerà direttamente a Clifton per cenare lì; e non appena finita la cena…

È finito; se c’è ancora [[motifs/time|tempo]], andiamo avanti verso Kingsweston.



“Dubito che riusciremo a fare tanto,” disse Morland.



“Maledetto vecchio!” gridò Thorpe. “Riusciremo a farne dieci volte di più…”

Di più. Kingsweston! Sì, anche Blaize [[settings/castle|Castello]], e qualsiasi altra cosa possiamo ottenere.

“Ne ho sentito parlare, ma tua sorella dice che non vuole andare.”



“Blaize [[settings/castle|Castle]]!”, gridò Catherine. “Che cos’è quello?”



“Il posto più bello d’Inghilterra: vale la pena percorrere cinquanta miglia in qualsiasi momento per, ”

“Vedi…”



“Che cosa, è davvero un [[settings/castle|castello]], un vecchio [[settings/castle|castello]]?”



“Il più anziano del regno.”



“Ma è davvero come si legge nei libri?”



Esattamente… proprio lo stesso.



“Ma ora davvero… esistono torri e lunghi corridoi?”



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_12--part_02" data-title="Northanger Abbey — Chapter 11 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 12" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/horse,motif/night,motif/road,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,motif/winter,concept/hope,setting/castle,character/isabella"></span>


“By dozens.”



“Then I should like to see it; but I cannot—I cannot go.”



“Not go! my beloved creature, what do you mean?”



“I cannot go, because”—looking down as she spoke, fearful of [[characters/isabella|Isabella]]’s

smile—“I expect Miss Tilney and her brother to call on me to take a

country walk. They promised to come at twelve, only it rained; but now,

as it is so fine, I dare say they will be here soon.”



“Not they indeed,” cried Thorpe; “for, as we turned into Broad Street,

I saw them—does he not drive a phaeton with bright chestnuts?”



“I do not know indeed.”



“Yes, I know he does; I saw him. You are talking of the man you danced

with last [[motifs/night|night]], are not you?”



“Yes.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], I saw him at that moment turn up the Lansdown [[motifs/road|Road]], driving a

smart-looking girl.”



“Did you indeed?”



“Did upon my [[motifs/soul|soul]]; knew him again directly, and he seemed to have got

some very pretty cattle too.”



“It is very odd! but I suppose they thought it would be too dirty for a

walk.”



“And [[motifs/well|well]] they might, for I never saw so much dirt in my life. Walk!

You could no more walk than you could fly! it has not been so dirty the

whole [[motifs/winter|winter]]; it is ankle-deep everywhere.”



[[characters/isabella|Isabella]] corroborated it: “My dearest Catherine, you cannot form an

idea of the dirt; come, you must go; you cannot refuse going now.”



“I should like to see the [[settings/castle|castle]]; but may we go all over it? May we go

up every staircase, and into every suite of rooms?”



“Yes, yes, every hole and corner.”



“But then, if they should only be gone out for an hour till it is

dryer, and call by and by?”



“Make yourself easy, there is no danger of that, for I heard Tilney

hallooing to a man who was just passing by on horseback, that they were

going as far as Wick Rocks.”



“Then I will. Shall I go, Mrs. Allen?”



“Just as you please, my dear.”



“Mrs. Allen, you must persuade her to go,” was the general cry. Mrs.

Allen was not inattentive to it: “[[motifs/well|Well]], my dear,” said she, “suppose

you go.” And in two minutes they were off.



Catherine’s feelings, as she got into the carriage, were in a very

unsettled state; divided between regret for the loss of one great

pleasure, and the [[concepts/hope|hope]] of soon enjoying another, almost its equal in

degree, however unlike in kind. She could not think the Tilneys had

acted quite [[motifs/well|well]] by her, in so readily giving up their engagement,

without sending her any message of excuse. It was now but an hour later

than the [[motifs/time|time]] fixed on for the beginning of their walk; and, in spite

of what she had heard of the prodigious accumulation of dirt in the

course of that hour, she could not from her own observation help

thinking that they might have gone with very little inconvenience. To

feel herself slighted by them was very painful. On the other hand, the

delight of exploring an edifice like Udolpho, as her fancy represented

Blaize [[settings/castle|Castle]] to be, was such a counterpoise of good as might console

her for almost anything.



They passed briskly down Pulteney Street, and through Laura Place,

without the exchange of many words. Thorpe talked to his [[motifs/horse|horse]], and she

meditated, by turns, on broken promises and broken arches, phaetons and

false hangings, Tilneys and trap-doors. As they entered Argyle

Buildings, however, she was roused by this address from her companion,

“Who is that girl who looked at you so hard as she went by?”



“Who? Where?”



“On the right-hand pavement—she must be almost out of sight now.”

Catherine looked round and saw Miss Tilney leaning on her brother’s

arm, walking slowly down the street. She saw them both looking back at

her. “Stop, stop, Mr. Thorpe,” she impatiently cried; “it is Miss

Tilney; it is indeed. How could you tell me they were gone? Stop, stop,

I will get out this moment and go to them.” But to what purpose did she

speak? Thorpe only lashed his [[motifs/horse|horse]] into a brisker trot; the Tilneys,

who had soon ceased to look after her, were in a moment out of sight

round the corner of Laura Place, and in another moment she was herself

whisked into the marketplace. Still, however, and during the length of

another street, she entreated him to stop. “Pray, pray stop, Mr.

Thorpe. I cannot go on. I will not go on. I must go back to Miss

Tilney.” But Mr. Thorpe only laughed, smacked his whip, encouraged his

[[motifs/horse|horse]], made odd noises, and drove on; and Catherine, angry and vexed as

she was, having no power of getting away, was obliged to give up the

point and submit. Her reproaches, however, were not spared. “How could

you deceive me so, Mr. Thorpe? How could you say that you saw them

driving up the Lansdown [[motifs/road|Road]]? I would not have had it happen so for the

world. They must think it so strange, so rude of me! to go by them,

too, without saying a word! you do not know how vexed I am; I shall

have no pleasure at Clifton, nor in anything else. I had rather, ten

thousand times rather, get out now, and walk back to them. How could

you say you saw them driving out in a phaeton?” Thorpe defended himself

very stoutly, declared he had never seen two men so much alike in his

life, and would hardly give up the point of its having been Tilney

himself.



Their drive, even when this subject was over, was not likely to be very

agreeable. Catherine’s complaisance was no longer what it had been in

their former airing. She listened reluctantly, and her replies were

short. Blaize [[settings/castle|Castle]] remained her only comfort; towards _that_, she

still looked at intervals with pleasure; though rather than be

disappointed of the promised walk, and especially rather than be

thought ill of by the Tilneys, she would willingly have given up all

the happiness which its walls could supply—the happiness of a progress

through a long suite of lofty rooms, exhibiting the remains of

magnificent furniture, though now for many years deserted—the happiness

of being stopped in their way along narrow, winding vaults, by a low,


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

“Decine su decine.”



“Allora vorrei vederlo… ma non posso… non riesco ad andare.”



"Non andare! mia adorata creatura, cosa intendi?"



“Non posso andare, perché, ” – mentre parlava, guardava verso il basso, temendo la reazione di [[characters/isabella|Isabella]].

Sorridi… “Mi aspetto che la signorina Tilney e suo fratello vengano a trovarmi per…”

Passeggiata campestre. Avevano promesso di arrivare alle dodici, ma ha piovuto… Ora…

“Poiché è così bella, oserei dire che arriveranno presto.”



“Assolutamente no,” esclamò Thorpe; “perché, non appena svoltammo in Broad Street…”

“Li ho visti… Non guida forse una carrozza con ruote color castagna scura?”



“Non lo so davvero.”



"Sì, so che lo fa; l’ho visto con i miei occhi. Stai parlando di quell’uomo con cui hai ballato..."

Con l’ultima [[motifs/night|notte]], non è vero?



“Sì, davvero.”



“Beh, l’ho visto in quel momento arrivare su Lansdown Road, guidando una, ”

“Una ragazza dall’aspetto attraente.”



“Davvero lo hai fatto?”



“Affezionò la mia [[motifs/soul|'anima]]; lo riconobbi di nuovo direttamente, e sembrava che avesse, ”

“Anche alcune mucche davvero molto belle.”



“È molto strano… Ma immagino che pensassero che sarebbe stato troppo sporco per…”

“Cammina.”



“E beh, potrebbero anche farlo, perché non ho mai visto così tanta sporcizia in vita mia. Andiamo!”

Non si poteva camminare, né volare… Non era mai stato così sporco prima.

L’intero [[motifs/winter|inverno]]; ovunque l’acqua arriva alle caviglie.”



[[characters/isabella|Isabella]] lo confermò: “Mia cara Catherine, non puoi formare un, ”

“Non hai altra scelta: devi andare, non puoi rifiutare.”



“Mi piacerebbe vedere il [[settings/castle|castello]]; ma possiamo visitarlo completamente? Possiamo, ”

“Su ogni scala, in ogni suite di stanze…”



"Sì, sì, in ogni angolo e recesso."



“Ma allora, se dovessero uscire solo per un’ora, fino a quando…”

"Asciugacapelli… e poi verrai a trovarmi più tardi?”



“Non preoccuparti, non c’è alcun pericolo… perché ho sentito dire che Tilney…”

"Salutando un uomo che stava appena passando a cavallo, per fargli sapere che..."

“Arrivare fino a Wick Rocks.”



“Allora lo farò. Devo andare, signora Allen?”



“Come desideri tu, mio caro.”



“Signora Allen, deve convincerla ad andare”, era il grido generale. Signora Allen.

Allen non era indifferente a questa questione: “[[motifs/well|Beh]], caro mio,” disse lei, “supponiamo, ”

“Vai pure.” E in due minuti se ne andarono.



I sentimenti di Catherine, mentre saliva nella carrozza, erano davvero…

Stato di instabilità; diviso tra rimpianti per la perdita di qualcosa di grande…

Piacere, e la [[concepts/hope|>speranza]] di poter presto godere di un altro, quasi altrettanto bello.

Titolo:  
Un grado di differenza, anche se sostanziale… Non riusciva a pensare che i Tilney fossero diversi in quel senso.

Si è comportata davvero bene, rinunciando così facilmente al loro fidanzamento.

Senza inviarle alcuna scusa. Era trascorso soltanto un’ora.

Prima dell’ora stabilita per l’inizio della loro passeggiata; e nonostante ciò.

Titolo:  
Di quanto aveva sentito riguardo all’enorme accumulo di sporcizia…

Durante quell’ora, non poté fare a meno di osservare…

Pensando che avrebbero potuto farlo con pochissimi inconvenienti…

Sentirsi trascurata da loro era davvero doloroso. D’altra parte…

Il piacere di esplorare un edificio come Udolpho, così come la sua immaginazione lo rappresentava…

Blaize [[settings/castle|Castle]], per natura sua, rappresentava un contrappeso di bontà in grado di consolare chiunque.

Per quasi qualsiasi cosa, lei era disposta a farlo.



Attraversarono rapidamente Pulteney Street e poi Laura Place

Senza scambiare molte parole, Thorpe parlò con il suo [[motifs/horse|cavallo]], e quello.

Rifletté, a turno, sulle promesse mancate e sugli archi spezzati, sui faitoni…

False hangings, Tilneys e porte segrete: così entrarono ad Argyle

Edifici… ma fu proprio questo discorso del suo compagno a svegliarla.

“Chi è quella ragazza che ti ha guardato in quel modo mentre passava?”



“Chi? Dove?”



Sul marciapiede di destra… ormai deve essere quasi sparita dalla vista.

Catherine guardò intorno e vide Miss Tilney appoggiata al fratello di lei.

Camminando lentamente per la strada… Li vide entrambi voltarsi indietro.

“Fermatevi, fermatevi, signor Thorpe”, gridò lei impazientemente; “è la signorina…”

Tilney… davvero. Come hai potuto dirmi che se n’erano andati? Fermati, fermati.

“Uscirò immediatamente e andrò da loro… Ma a quale scopo?”

Parlare? Thorpe si limitò ad incitare il suo [[motifs/horse|cavallo]] ad accelerare il passo; i Tilney.

Coloro che un tempo si prendevano cura di lei, in un attimo scomparvero dalla sua vista.

Dietro l’angolo di Laura Place… e in un attimo, lei stessa fu di nuovo lì.

Portato immediatamente sul mercato. Tuttavia, per tutto il periodo…

In un'altra strada, lo pregò di fermarsi. “Per favore, si fermi, signore, ”

Thorpe… Non posso andare avanti… Non voglio andare avanti… Devo tornare da Miss…

“Tilney…” Ma il signor Thorpe si limitò a ridere, schioccò la frusta e incoraggiò il suo cavallo.

Il [[motifs/horse|cavallo]] emetteva suoni strani, ma continuava a camminare; e Catherine, arrabbiata e infastidita.

Non aveva alcuna possibilità di fuggire, quindi fu costretta ad arrendersi

“Punta e consegna… Ma le sue rimproveri non le furono risparmiati. ‘Come hai potuto…’”

Mi inganni davvero così, signor Thorpe? Come avete potuto dire di averli visti?

Guidando su per la Lansdown [[motifs/road|Strada]]? Non avrei voluto che accadesse, quindi.

Il mondo… Devono pensare che sia così strano, così scortese da parte mia, passargli accanto senza fermarmi.

Anche tu, senza dire una parola… Non sai quanto io sia infastidita; non so proprio cosa fare…

“Non provo alcun piacere a Clifton, né in nulla altro… Preferirei di dieci volte…”

Mille volte meglio… Vai subito da loro e torna indietro con loro. Come potresti…

“Dici di averli visti andarsene in una phaeton?” si difese Thorpe.

Con fermezza dichiarò di non aver mai visto due uomini così simili in tutta la sua vita.

Titolo:  
La vita… e difficilmente si rinuncerebbe allo scopo per cui è stata creata… fino a Tilney.

Se stesso.



La loro determinazione, anche dopo che l’argomento era stato trattato, probabilmente non sarebbe diminuita molto.

Aggradabile… La sottomissione di Catherine non era più quella di un tempo.

La sua precedente trasmissione… Ascoltò con riluttanza, e le sue risposte furono…

In breve. Blaize [[settings/castle|Castle]] rimase l’unico conforto per lei; verso di essa, lei.

Ancora lo guardava di tanto in tanto con piacere; anche se, piuttosto che…

Deluso dalla passeggiata promessa… e soprattutto, piuttosto che…

Sebbene i Tilney la considerassero negativamente, lei avrebbe volentieri rinunciato a tutto.

La felicità che quei muri potevano offrire… la felicità di un percorso di crescita.

Attraverso una lunga serie di stanze imponenti, si possono ammirare i resti di…

Mobili magnifici, sebbene da molti anni abbandonati… La felicità.

Intralci lungo passaggi stretti e tortuosi…



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_12--part_03" data-title="Northanger Abbey — Chapter 11 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 12" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/fool,motif/horse,motif/journey,motif/night,motif/tears,motif/well,motif/wind,concept/wonder,character/isabella"></span>


grated door; or even of having their lamp, their only lamp,

extinguished by a sudden gust of [[motifs/wind|wind]], and of being left in total

darkness. In the meanwhile, they proceeded on their [[motifs/journey|journey]] without any

mischance, and were within view of the town of Keynsham, when a halloo

from Morland, who was behind them, made his friend pull up, to know

what was the matter. The others then came close enough for

conversation, and Morland said, “We had better go back, Thorpe; it is

too late to go on to-day; your sister thinks so as [[motifs/well|well]] as I. We have

been exactly an hour coming from Pulteney Street, very little more than

seven miles; and, I suppose, we have at least eight more to go. It will

never do. We set out a great deal too late. We had much better put it

off till another day, and turn round.”



“It is all one to me,” replied Thorpe rather angrily; and instantly

turning his [[motifs/horse|horse]], they were on their way back to Bath.



“If your brother had not got such a d—— beast to drive,” said he soon

afterwards, “we might have done it very [[motifs/well|well]]. My [[motifs/horse|horse]] would have

trotted to Clifton within the hour, if left to himself, and I have

almost broke my arm with pulling him in to that cursed broken-winded

jade’s pace. Morland is a [[archetypes/fool|fool]] for not keeping a [[motifs/horse|horse]] and gig of his

own.”



“No, he is not,” said Catherine warmly, “for I am sure he could not

afford it.”



“And why cannot he afford it?”



“Because he has not money enough.”



“And whose fault is that?”



“Nobody’s, that I know of.” Thorpe then said something in the loud,

incoherent way to which he had often recourse, about its being a

d—— thing to be miserly; and that if people who rolled in money could not

afford things, he did not know who could, which Catherine did not even

endeavour to understand. Disappointed of what was to have been the

consolation for her first disappointment, she was less and less

disposed either to be agreeable herself or to find her companion so;

and they returned to Pulteney Street without her speaking twenty words.



As she entered the house, the footman told her that a gentleman and

lady had called and inquired for her a few minutes after her setting

off; that, when he told them she was gone out with Mr. Thorpe, the lady

had asked whether any message had been left for her; and on his saying

no, had felt for a card, but said she had none about her, and went

away. Pondering over these heart-rending tidings, Catherine walked

slowly upstairs. At the head of them she was met by Mr. Allen, who, on

hearing the reason of their speedy return, said, “I am glad your

brother had so much sense; I am glad you are come back. It was a

strange, wild scheme.”



They all spent the evening together at Thorpe’s. Catherine was

disturbed and out of spirits; but [[characters/isabella|Isabella]] seemed to find a pool of

commerce, in the fate of which she shared, by private partnership with

Morland, a very good equivalent for the quiet and country air of an inn

at Clifton. Her satisfaction, too, in not being at the Lower Rooms was

spoken more than once. “How I pity the poor creatures that are going

there! how glad I am that I am not amongst them! i [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] whether it

will be a full ball or not! they have not begun dancing yet. I would

not be there for all the world. It is so delightful to have an evening

now and then to oneself. I dare say it will not be a very good ball. I

know the Mitchells will not be there. I am sure I pity everybody that

is. But I dare say, Mr. Morland, you long to be at it, do not you? I am

sure you do. [[motifs/well|Well]], pray do not let anybody here be a restraint on you.

I dare say we could do very [[motifs/well|well]] without you; but you men think

yourselves of such consequence.”



Catherine could almost have accused [[characters/isabella|Isabella]] of being wanting in

tenderness towards herself and her sorrows, so very little did they

appear to dwell on her mind, and so very inadequate was the comfort she

offered. “Do not be so dull, my dearest creature,” she whispered. “You

will quite break my heart. It was amazingly shocking, to be sure; but

the Tilneys were entirely to blame. Why were not they more punctual? It

was dirty, indeed, but what did that signify? I am sure John and I

should not have minded it. I never mind going through anything, where a

friend is concerned; that is my disposition, and John is just the same;

he has amazing strong feelings. Good heavens! what a delightful hand

you have got! kings, I vow! i never was so happy in my life! i would

fifty times rather you should have them than myself.”



And now I may dismiss my heroine to the sleepless couch, which is the

true heroine’s portion; to a pillow strewed with thorns and wet with

[[motifs/tears|tears]]. And lucky may she think herself, if she get another good [[motifs/night|night]]’s

rest in the course of the next three months.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Porta grattugiata… o addirittura la loro unica lampada…

Scomparso improvvisamente a causa di un forte soffio di [[motifs/wind|>vento]], rimase completamente abbandonato.

Oscurità. Nel frattempo, continuarono il loro [[motifs/journey|Viaggio]] senza alcun intoppo.

“Mischance… e mentre erano in vista della città di Keynsham, qualcuno gridò ‘Ehi!’”

Da parte di Morland, che si trovava dietro di loro, chiese al suo amico di fermarsi, per sapere…

Che cosa era successo… Gli altri si avvicinarono abbastanza da poter vedere…

“Dovremmo tornare indietro, Thorpe; è meglio così.”

È troppo tardi per andare oggi; anche tua sorella la pensa così, proprio come me. Abbiamo.

È passata esattamente un’ora da quando sono partito da Pulteney Street…

Sette miglia… e immagino che ci restino almeno altre otto da percorrere.

Mai farlo. Siamo partiti troppo tardi; sarebbe stato meglio procedere prima.

“Per ora basta, e riprenderemo un’altra volta.”



“Per me è tutto lo stesso”, rispose Thorpe con una certa irritazione; e immediatamente…

Mettendo in movimento il loro [[motifs/horse|cavallo]], si diressero verso casa, a Bath.



“Se tuo fratello non avesse avuto un animale così maledetto da guidare…”, disse presto.

In seguito, “avremmo potuto farcela molto bene. Il mio [[motifs/horse|cavallo]] avrebbe, ”.

In un’ora al massimo sarebbe arrivato a Clifton, se gli fosse stato lasciato fare…

Quasi mi rompevo il braccio trascinandolo dentro quel maledetto posto…

Il passo lento di Jade. Morland è un [[archetypes/fool|idiota]] per non possedere nemmeno un cavallo o una carrozza tutta sua.

“Proprio.”



“No, non lo è,” disse Catherine con calore, “perché sono sicura che non ne sarebbe in grado.”

“Non te lo puoi permettere.”



“E perché non può permetterselo?”



“Perché non ha abbastanza soldi.”



“E di chi è la colpa?”



“Nessuno, per quel che ne so,” disse poi Thorpe ad alta voce.

Un modo incoerente al quale spesso ricorreva, riguardo al fatto che fosse…

Essere avari non è certo una cosa lodevole… E soprattutto, se coloro che hanno montagne di denaro non fossero capaci di…

“Non sapeva chi fosse in grado di permettersi certe cose… E nemmeno Catherine lo sapeva.”

Cercare di capire… Deluso da ciò che avrebbe dovuto essere

Consolazione per la sua prima delusione… diventava sempre meno…

Disposta o ad essere piacevole lei stessa, o a rendere il proprio compagno tale.

E tornarono in Pulteney Street senza che lei pronunciasse nemmeno venti parole.



Non appena entrò nella casa, il maggiordomo le disse che c'era un gentiluomo e.

La signora aveva chiamato e chiesto di lei pochi minuti dopo che se n’era andata.

“Off; quando disse loro che era uscita con il signor Thorpe, la signora…”

Aveva chiesto se le fosse stata lasciata qualche messaggio; e quando lui rispose…

“No, aveva desiderato ricevere una cartolina, ma disse di non averne nessuna con sé e se ne andò.”

Lontano… Mentre rifletteva su queste notizie strazianti, Catherine camminava…

Lentamente su per le scale… In cima ad esse fu accolta dal signor Allen, che…

“Dopo aver ascoltato le ragioni del vostro rapido ritorno, dissi: ‘Sono felice che siate tornati.’”

“Mio fratello aveva davvero molto buon senso… Sono felice che tu sia tornato.”

“Un piano strano e folle.”



Tutti trascorsero la serata insieme da Thorpe. Catherine…

Disturbato e senza spirito, ma [[characters/isabella|Isabella]] sembrava aver trovato un po’ di conforto.

Titolo:  
Il commercio, nel cui destino lei fu coinvolta attraverso una partnership privata…

Morland: l’equivalente ideale di quell’atmosfera tranquilla e rurale tipica di una locanda

A Clifton… Anche lei era soddisfatta di non trovarsi nelle “Lower Rooms”.

“Come mi dispiacciono quelle povere creature che stanno per…” – detto più volte.

Ecco! Che sollievo sapere di non essere tra loro. Mi chiedo se.

Sarà davvero una festa in pieno svolgimento… o no? Non hanno ancora iniziato a ballare. Io direi…

Non essere presente in tutto il mondo… È davvero delizioso trascorrere una serata così.

Ogni tanto, ci si ritrova a pensare a se stessi… Oserei dire che non sarà certo una bella festa.

“So che i Mitchell non saranno lì… Sono sicuro di provare compassione per tutti quelli…”

“Ma oserei dire, signor Morland, che non vediate l’ora di iniziare, vero? Io sì…”

Certo che lo fai. [[motifs/well|Beh]], spero davvero che nessuno qui possa rappresentare un ostacolo per te.

Oso dire che potremmo cavarcela molto bene senza di te; ma voi uomini pensate diversamente.

“Ricordate bene le conseguenze di tali azioni.”



Catherine avrebbe quasi potuto accusare [[characters/isabella|Isabella]] di voler intervenire.

Tenerezza verso se stessa e le proprie sofferenze… così poca, in realtà.

Sembrava che quel pensiero non la lasciasse mai in pace; e il conforto che riusciva a trovarsi era davvero assai insufficiente…

“Non essere così noiosa, mia adorata creatura,” sussurrò. “Tu…”

Mi spezzerà davvero il cuore… È stato davvero scioccante, senza dubbio; ma…

I Tilney erano completamente da biasimare… Perché non erano più puntuali?

Era sporco, davvero, ma cosa significava? Sono sicura che io e John…

Non avrei dovuto farci caso… Non mi dispiace affatto affrontare qualsiasi situazione, purché sia necessaria.

Un amico è preoccupato… Questa è la mia natura, e lo stesso vale per John.

Sentimenti intensi e profondi… Che mano deliziosa!

Mai stato così felice!

“Cinquanta volte meglio che le avessi tu piuttosto che io.”



E ora posso lasciare la mia eroina sul divano insonne…

La sorte della vera eroina: un cuscino coperto di spine e bagnato…

[[Tears|[lacrime]]]. E possa considerarsi fortunata, se riesce a trascorrere un'altra buona [[motifs/night|notte]].

Avverrà nel corso dei prossimi tre mesi.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_13" data-title="Northanger Abbey — Chapter 12" data-chapter="Chapter 13" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="motif/home,motif/night,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,motif/window,concept/doubt,concept/fear,concept/honour,form/comedy,setting/london,character/bottom,character/edgar,character/eleanor,character/general_tilney,character/henry_tilney,character/isabella,character/john_thorpe"></span>


CHAPTER 12





“Mrs. Allen,” said Catherine the next morning, “will there be any harm

in my calling on Miss Tilney to-day? I shall not be easy till I have

explained everything.”



“Go, by all means, my dear; only put on a white gown; Miss Tilney

always wears white.”



Catherine cheerfully complied, and being properly equipped, was more

impatient than ever to be at the pump-room, that she might inform

herself of [[characters/general-tilney|General Tilney]]’s lodgings, for though she believed they were

in Milsom Street, she was not certain of the house, and Mrs. Allen’s

wavering convictions only made it more doubtful. To Milsom Street she

was directed, and having made herself perfect in the number, hastened

away with eager steps and a beating heart to pay her visit, explain her

conduct, and be forgiven; tripping lightly through the church-yard, and

resolutely turning away her eyes, that she might not be obliged to see

her beloved [[characters/isabella|Isabella]] and her dear family, who, she had reason to

believe, were in a shop hard by. She reached the house without any

impediment, looked at the number, knocked at the door, and inquired for

Miss Tilney. The man believed Miss Tilney to be at [[motifs/home|home]], but was not

quite certain. Would she be pleased to send up her name? She gave her

card. In a few minutes the servant returned, and with a look which did

not quite confirm his words, said he had been mistaken, for that Miss

Tilney was walked out. Catherine, with a blush of mortification, left

the house. She felt almost persuaded that Miss Tilney _was_ at [[motifs/home|home]],

and too much offended to admit her; and as she retired down the street,

could not withhold one glance at the drawing-room windows, in

expectation of seeing her there, but no one appeared at them. At the

[[characters/bottom|bottom]] of the street, however, she looked back again, and then, not at

a [[motifs/window|window]], but issuing from the door, she saw Miss Tilney herself. She

was followed by a gentleman, whom Catherine believed to be her father,

and they turned up towards [[characters/edgar|Edgar]]’s Buildings. Catherine, in deep

mortification, proceeded on her way. She could almost be angry herself

at such angry incivility; but she checked the resentful sensation; she

remembered her own ignorance. She knew not how such an offence as hers

might be classed by the laws of worldly politeness, to what a degree of

unforgivingness it might with propriety lead, nor to what rigours of

rudeness in return it might justly make her amenable.



Dejected and humbled, she had even some thoughts of not going with the

others to the theatre that [[motifs/night|night]]; but it must be confessed that they

were not of long continuance, for she soon recollected, in the first

place, that she was without any excuse for staying at [[motifs/home|home]]; and, in the

second, that it was a play she wanted very much to see. To the theatre

accordingly they all went; no Tilneys appeared to plague or please her;

she feared that, amongst the many perfections of the family, a fondness

for plays was not to be ranked; but perhaps it was because they were

habituated to the finer performances of the [[settings/london|London]] stage, which she

knew, on [[characters/isabella|Isabella]]’s authority, rendered everything else of the kind

“quite horrid.” She was not deceived in her own expectation of

pleasure; the [[forms/comedy|comedy]] so [[motifs/well|well]] suspended her care that no one, observing

her during the first four acts, would have supposed she had any

wretchedness about her. On the beginning of the fifth, however, the

sudden view of Mr. [[characters/henry-tilney|Henry Tilney]] and his father, joining a party in the

opposite box, recalled her to anxiety and distress. The stage could no

longer excite genuine merriment—no longer keep her whole attention.

Every other look upon an average was directed towards the opposite box;

and, for the space of two entire scenes, did she thus watch Henry

Tilney, without being once able to catch his eye. No longer could he be

suspected of indifference for a play; his notice was never withdrawn

from the stage during two whole scenes. At length, however, he did look

towards her, and he bowed—but such a bow! no smile, no continued

observance attended it; his eyes were immediately returned to their

former direction. Catherine was restlessly miserable; she could almost

have run round to the box in which he sat and forced him to hear her

explanation. Feelings rather natural than heroic possessed her; instead

of considering her own dignity injured by this ready

condemnation—instead of proudly resolving, in conscious innocence, to

show her resentment towards him who could harbour a [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] of it, to

leave to him all the trouble of seeking an explanation, and to

enlighten him on the past only by avoiding his sight, or flirting with

somebody else—she took to herself all the shame of misconduct, or at

least of its appearance, and was only eager for an opportunity of

explaining its cause.



The play concluded—the curtain fell—[[characters/henry-tilney|Henry Tilney]] was no longer to be

seen where he had hitherto sat, but his father remained, and perhaps he

might be now coming round to their box. She was right; in a few minutes

he appeared, and, making his way through the then thinning rows, spoke

with like calm politeness to Mrs. Allen and her friend. Not with such

calmness was he answered by the latter: “Oh! mr. Tilney, I have been

quite wild to speak to you, and make my apologies. You must have

thought me so rude; but indeed it was not my own fault, was it, Mrs.

Allen? Did not they tell me that Mr. Tilney and his sister were gone

out in a phaeton together? And then what could I do? But I had ten

thousand times rather have been with you; now had not I, Mrs. Allen?”



“My dear, you tumble my gown,” was Mrs. Allen’s reply.



Her assurance, however, standing sole as it did, was not thrown away;

it brought a more cordial, more natural smile into his countenance, and

he replied in a tone which retained only a little affected reserve: “We

were much obliged to you at any rate for wishing us a pleasant walk

after our passing you in Argyle Street: you were so kind as to look

back on purpose.”



“But indeed I did not wish you a pleasant walk; I never thought of such

a thing; but I begged Mr. Thorpe so earnestly to stop; I called out to

him as soon as ever I saw you; now, Mrs. Allen, did not—Oh! you were

not there; but indeed I did; and, if Mr. Thorpe would only have

stopped, I would have jumped out and run after you.”



Is there a Henry in the world who could be insensible to such a

declaration? [[characters/henry-tilney|Henry Tilney]] at least was not. With a yet sweeter smile,

he said everything that need be said of his sister’s concern, regret,

and dependence on Catherine’s [[concepts/honour|honour]]. “Oh, do not say Miss Tilney was

not angry,” cried Catherine, “because I know she was; for she would not

see me this morning when I called; I saw her walk out of the house the

next minute after my leaving it; I was hurt, but I was not affronted.

Perhaps you did not know I had been there.”



“I was not within at the [[motifs/time|time]]; but I heard of it from [[characters/eleanor|Eleanor]], and she

has been wishing ever since to see you, to explain the reason of such

incivility; but perhaps I can do it as [[motifs/well|well]]. It was nothing more than

that my father—they were just preparing to walk out, and he being

hurried for [[motifs/time|time]], and not caring to have it put off—made a point of her

being denied. That was all, I do assure you. She was very much vexed,

and meant to make her apology as soon as possible.”



Catherine’s mind was greatly eased by this information, yet a something

of solicitude remained, from which sprang the following question,

thoroughly artless in itself, though rather distressing to the

gentleman: “But, Mr. Tilney, why were _you_ less generous than your

sister? If she felt such confidence in my good intentions, and could

suppose it to be only a mistake, why should _you_ be so ready to take

offence?”



“Me! i take offence!”



“Nay, I am sure by your look, when you came into the box, you were

angry.”



“I angry! i could have no right.”



“[[motifs/well|Well]], nobody would have thought you had no right who saw your face.”

He replied by asking her to make room for him, and talking of the play.



He remained with them some [[motifs/time|time]], and was only too agreeable for

Catherine to be contented when he went away. Before they parted,

however, it was agreed that the projected walk should be taken as soon

as possible; and, setting aside the misery of his quitting their box,

she was, upon the whole, left one of the happiest creatures in the

world.



While talking to each other, she had observed with some surprise that

[[characters/john-thorpe|John Thorpe]], who was never in the same part of the house for ten

minutes together, was engaged in conversation with [[characters/general-tilney|General Tilney]]; and

she felt something more than surprise when she thought she could

perceive herself the object of their attention and discourse. What

could they have to say of her? She feared [[characters/general-tilney|General Tilney]] did not like

her appearance: she found it was implied in his preventing her

admittance to his daughter, rather than postpone his own walk a few

minutes. “How came Mr. Thorpe to know your father?” was her anxious

inquiry, as she pointed them out to her companion. He knew nothing

about it; but his father, like every military man, had a very large

acquaintance.



When the entertainment was over, Thorpe came to assist them in getting

out. Catherine was the immediate object of his gallantry; and, while

they waited in the lobby for a chair, he prevented the inquiry which

had travelled from her heart almost to the tip of her tongue, by

asking, in a consequential manner, whether she had seen him talking

with [[characters/general-tilney|General Tilney]]: “He is a fine old fellow, upon my [[motifs/soul|soul]]! stout,

active—looks as young as his son. I have a great regard for him, I

assure you: a gentleman-like, good sort of fellow as ever lived.”



“But how came you to know him?”



“Know him! there are few people much about town that I do not know. I

have met him forever at the Bedford; and I knew his face again to-day

the moment he came into the billiard-room. One of the best players we

have, by the by; and we had a little touch together, though I was

almost afraid of him at first: the odds were five to four against me;

and, if I had not made one of the cleanest strokes that perhaps ever

was made in this world—I took his ball exactly—but I could not make you

understand it without a table; however, I _did_ beat him. A very fine

fellow; as rich as a Jew. I should like to dine with him; I dare say he

gives famous dinners. But what do you think we have been talking of?

You. Yes, by heavens! and the General thinks you the finest girl in

Bath.”



“Oh! nonsense! how can you say so?”



“And what do you think I said?”—lowering his voice—“[[motifs/well|well]] done, General,

said I; I am quite of your mind.”



Here Catherine, who was much less gratified by his admiration than by

[[characters/general-tilney|General Tilney]]’s, was not sorry to be called away by Mr. Allen. Thorpe,

however, would see her to her chair, and, till she entered it,

continued the same kind of delicate flattery, in spite of her

entreating him to have done.



That [[characters/general-tilney|General Tilney]], instead of disliking, should admire her, was very

delightful; and she joyfully thought that there was not one of the

family whom she need now [[concepts/fear|fear]] to meet. The evening had done more, much

more, for her than could have been expected.
